name: The Fernleaf Beech of Palazzo Doria-Tursi
age_estimate: roughly 100-180 years (girth-based estimate, no dated source)

location.address: Via Garibaldi 9, 16124 Genova (courtyard of Palazzo Doria-Tursi)
location.neighbourhood: Via Garibaldi / Strada Nuova, historic centre

verified_sources: https://cultura.gov.it (MASAF national monumental trees register, sheet 09/D969/GE/07, girth 230cm, height 21m)
access: Free. Stands in the courtyard of Palazzo Doria-Tursi, a Rolli palace (UNESCO) that now houses Genoa's city hall and the Strada Nuova Museums; the main courtyard and staircase are generally open to the public without a ticket during opening hours, per general sourcing on the palace. Not personally confirmed the tree itself is unobstructed from the courtyard this pass.
transport: In the pedestrianised heart of Via Garibaldi, a few minutes' walk from Genova De Ferrari / San Giorgio
verify_notes: Register calls it 'faggio a foglie di asplenio', a fern-leaved cultivar of European beech, cut-leaved and lacy compared to the ordinary species; a real oddity to find inside a 16th-century palace courtyard rather than a park. GenovaToday's Dec 2023 piece on the national monumental-tree map (its sixth update) names this exact tree by location, confirming it independently of the register. No source gives a planting date or age; the 100-180yr range is a rough estimate from girth alone (diameter ~73cm) and should be treated as indicative only, not sourced. Palazzo Doria-Tursi: built 1565 for Niccolò Grimaldi, passed to the Doria family 1596, bought by the Republic of Genoa, seat of Genoa's city government since 1848 - a possible planting-era anchor (post-1848 courtyard planting) but this is inference, not a source. Worth a photo/access check before publishing: confirm the tree is visible from the public part of the courtyard.

name: The Poet's Holm Oak of Montesignano
age_estimate: roughly 150-300 years (girth-based estimate, no dated source)

location.address: Via Mogadiscio 10, Montesignano, Genova (near the church of San Michele Arcangelo)
location.neighbourhood: Montesignano / San Desiderio, eastern hills of Genoa

verified_sources: https://cultura.gov.it (MASAF national monumental trees register, sheet 06/D969/GE/07, girth 257cm, height 15m)

Liguria regional monumental-tree register PDF (agriligurianet.it, 'Elenco regionale degli alberi monumentali'), same sheet 06/D969/GE/07, same girth 257cm/height 15m, locality given as 'Montesignano chiesa S. Michele arcangelo', criterion 'g) valore storico, culturale, religioso'
https://www.genovatoday.it/cronaca/la-mappa-degli-alberi-monumentali-il-patrimonio-green-di-genova.html (names 'il leccio di via Mogadiscio citato dal poeta Camillo Sbarbaro')
access: Not confirmed this pass. Via Mogadiscio is a residential street in the Montesignano district; independent geocoding places it at roughly the same coordinates as the register (44.4389, 8.9665), and the Liguria regional listing ties the tree to the church of San Michele Arcangelo rather than a private garden, which is a good sign, but I did not find a source stating the tree stands on public ground or is visible from the street. A local civic-tech initiative is literally named 'Il Leccio di via Mogadiscio' after it (Genova Digitale ran information sessions there), which suggests it functions as a known local landmark rather than a hidden private specimen, but that is not the same as confirmed public access.
transport: AMT bus lines 480/482, stop 'Mogadiscio 6/Giacalone', about 1 minute's walk from the stop; total time from the city centre not independently timed this pass, likely 20-30 minutes by bus
verify_notes: Register pitfall caught and resolved: the MASAF import (data/registers/italy-masaf.json) gives this tree's locality as 'Via Mogadiscio 10', while an older Liguria regional PDF snapshot of the SAME sheet ID (06/D969/GE/07, same girth 257cm, same height 15m) gives the locality as 'Montesignano chiesa S. Michele arcangelo'. This looked like a register conflict at first. It resolves: Via Mogadiscio is itself a street inside the Montesignano district near that church (confirmed via independent geocoding, ~44.4389/8.9665, a close match to the register coordinates) - so the two locality strings describe the same tree at two levels of specificity, not two different trees. Genoa poet and lichenologist Camillo Sbarbaro (1888-1967, author of 'Pianissimo') is reported to have referenced this specific oak; I could not find the actual line or poem title this pass, only the naming fact via GenovaToday, so the literary connection itself should be treated as a lead for the writer to verify against a primary Sbarbaro source before using as a quoted fact. Age not sourced by either register; Italy's national forestry register carries no age field for any entry, a known systemic gap, so the age range here is a rough girth estimate only.

verify_notes: Single-sourced: only the register was found. The girth (734cm, roughly 2.3m diameter) is exceptional for this species and far larger than the two other Cinnamomum glanduliferum specimens turned up elsewhere in this same pass (487cm at Villa Tigullio, Rapallo; 350-392cm at the two Villa Pallavicini locations), which is either a genuinely remarkable tree or a data-entry issue worth sanity-checking against a second measurement before publishing (per the register-pitfalls rule: check numbers against the physical world). If it verifies, it is a strong candidate on size alone; until then it should not be presented with any superlative claim (hard rule 8) and treat the girth itself as unconfirmed.

name: The Coast Redwood of Villa Serra
age_estimate: roughly 120-170 years (girth-based estimate consistent with the park's founding era, no dated source for this individual)

location.address: Parco Storico di Villa Serra, Via Carlo Levi 2, Comago, Sant'Olcese (GE)
location.neighbourhood: Comago, Sant'Olcese (Val Polcevera, Genoa metropolitan area, NOT within the comune of Genova)

verified_sources: https://cultura.gov.it (MASAF national monumental trees register, sheet 02/I346/GE/07, girth 526cm, height 38.5m)
https://www.villaserra.it/la-natura/gli-alberi/ (park's own site, confirms Sequoia sempervirens among the park's named specimens and gives species background)
access: Paid/managed historic park (Consorzio Villa Serra). Opening hours: Jan-Feb 10:00-17:00, Mar-Apr 10:00-18:00, May-Aug 09:00-20:00, Sep 09:00-19:00, Oct 10:00-18:00, Nov-Dec 10:00-17:00, Monday mornings closed.
transport: NOT in Genoa proper. Sant'Olcese/Comago is a separate comune in the Polcevera valley, roughly 9km north of Genoa's centre by road. Reachable by AMT bus lines 7, 735, 737, 738 (stop 'Comago/Scuola', 10-min walk, or 'L. Secca/Manesseno', 4-min walk), typically via a first leg to Genova Bolzaneto (train or bus) then a connecting local bus into the valley. I could not pin an exact door-to-door time this pass; it is plausibly close to or over the 30-minute day-trip threshold and should be timed properly, and labelled honestly as Sant'Olcese/Comago rather than presented as inside Genoa, per the day-trip boundary rule.
verify_notes: Part of a real four-tree walkable cluster: this Sequoia, the Cerro (gnv_006), the Carpino nero (gnv_007) and the Farnia (gnv_008) all sit within about 60 metres of each other inside Villa Serra's 9-hectare English park, per the register's own coordinates. This is genuinely the tightest cluster among all 14 candidates in the brief, tighter than the centro storico trio (which span 2-3.8km between each other, not really walkable as a set) and tighter than the Pegli pair. The catch is distance from central Genoa (see transport note) and that it is a different comune. Whether this counts as 'Genoa' or needs its own treatment is a call for whoever composes the city page, not settled here. Villa Serra's own site describes the park as established in the mid-19th century and reopened to the public in 1992 after restoration; the sequoia's age estimate follows from that planting era but is not independently dated for this specific tree the way the Carpino nero is (gnv_007 has an actual sourced age).
